title: Hosted API demo - chat & text generation basics
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Quantify Labs through hosted API chat/text basics: streaming, key generation params, retry behavior, and how to configure for latency vs cost. Customer cares mostly about predictable latency for real-time agent use, data retention/compliance, and cost. Agreed next steps: share pricing + SSO/Security docs, run a 1-week pilot with sample prompt set and benchmarking, and follow-up technical deep dive to scope Dedicated or Private if pilots show latency pain.

Samir Patel: Send sample benchmark script and suggested prompt set for Quantify Labs - due 2026-06-05
Priya Natarajan: Provide peak qps and typical prompt size examples - due 2026-06-04
next_steps: Redwood to send security pack (SOC2, ISO certs, data retention policies)
Customer to provide sample prompts and traffic profile
Agree SLA / success criteria for pilot (latency p50/p95 goals)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-02
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Natarajan (CTO, Quantify Labs), Marco Ruiz (ML Engineer), Dana Lee (Product)
---
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Alex from Redwood, i'll run through the hosted API demo today with Samir on the tech bits. how's everyone doing?
[00:08] Priya Natarajan: Good, thanks. excited to see what you have. we want to make sure the real-time agents we run get consistent latency.
[00:14] Alex Chen: totally - that's our focus. quick agenda: chat/text generation basics, streaming, major parameters you tweak (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop), then retries & idempotency + rate limits. we can dive deeper into dedicated/private after if needed.
[00:28] Samir Patel: also i'll show the console briefly, where you can inspect token costs and trace per-request latency.
[00:34] Marco Ruiz: great - our app is real-time, sub-300ms p50 ideally for short prompts, otherwise we fall back to async.
[00:41] Dana Lee: and team is sensitive to data retention - we can't have raw prompts logged for more than 30 days without approval.
[00:48] Alex Chen: noted. we have data retention options and customer-managed KMS for private. i'll flag security for the end. ok jumping into the demo.
[01:05] [screen share starts] Samir Patel: here is the simple POST /v1/chat/completions call in the Redwood hosted API. payload has model, messages, and stream=true for streaming responses.
[01:18] Samir Patel: (reads) example: { model: "redwood-mini-chat-v1", messages: [...], temperature: 0.2, stream: true } - streaming pushes tokens as they’re generated which helps perceived latency for chat use cases.
[01:32] Priya Natarajan: does streaming require websockets?
[01:35] Samir Patel: good question - we support chunked HTTP streaming and websockets; chunked is easiest for typical REST clients. we also expose SSE in some SDKs.
[01:45] Marco Ruiz: cool. does the streamed tokenization respect token boundaries well? we saw issues elsewhere where partial tokens get split oddly.
[01:51] Samir Patel: our token streaming is byte/utf-8 aware; occasional partial tokens in stream events can happen but SDKs buffer them so final text is clean. there are some ops tradeoffs with very small shards but generally fine.
[02:06] [00:02:06] Alex Chen: demoing parameters - temperature controls randomness, top_p as nucleus sampling; for reliable, deterministic responses you push temp to 0 or 0.0x and set top_p low.
[02:19] Priya Natarajan: for our agent, we want consistent action selection; probably temp=0.1 and top_p=0.9?
[02:24] Samir Patel: sounds reasonable. also consider max_tokens and response length. if you keep prompts short and cap responses you can hit lower latency and cost. our console shows token breakdown per call so you can tune.
[02:38] Dana Lee: how about stopping tokens? we have structured responses sometimes, want to enforce JSON only.
[02:43] Samir Patel: we support stop sequences and function-calling style structured outputs; you can also use our output validation hooks to reject non-JSON.
[02:53] [00:02:53] Marco Ruiz: retries - what is the recommended pattern for idempotency? our system will re-try network errors and want to avoid duplicate side-effects.
[03:00] Alex Chen: best practice is use idempotency keys at the application layer. Redwood's hosted API supports an Idempotency-Key header which will dedupe repeated requests within a short time window. for chat stream you should be careful to persist partial state.
[03:16] Priya Natarajan: what's the window?
[03:18] Samir Patel: default is 60 seconds for dedupe but you can request longer for dedicated/private installs.
[03:25] [00:03:25] Marco Ruiz: and retries on 5xx vs 429?
[03:28] Samir Patel: we recommend exponential backoff for 5xx. for 429 (rate limit), we return Retry-After header; best to respect that. Redwood also offers rate limit tiers and burst capacity with Dedicated.
[03:40] Alex Chen: quick note on graceful degradation - we can route to smaller models or cached responses when capacity is constrained; that'll help keep agents online with slightly lower quality.
[03:51] Priya Natarajan: acceptable as a fallback. question on cold-start for KV cache / long context - we have large web contexts sometimes.
[03:59] Samir Patel: we do prefix caching and KV cache to reuse key/value states for long conversations which reduces repeated compute. small caveat: for long initial contexts we may observe higher first-token latency.
[04:13] Dana Lee: any tuning you'd recommend for throughput vs latency?
[04:17] Samir Patel: yes - batching increases throughput and reduces per-token cost, but it introduces queuing latency. for strict p50 latency targets you set a small batch size and timeouts; console Optimize will suggest tradeoffs based on your observed distribution.
[04:33] [00:04:33] Alex Chen: switching to the console - here's per-route latency dashboards, token cost breakdown, and a trace for a single conversation. you can search by request id and see kernel choices (we pick optimized kernels by model and sequence length).
[04:49] Priya Natarajan: is kernel selection exposed? we want to understand quantized model variants chosen at run time.
[04:54] Samir Patel: we don't expose kernel internals to customers but we provide performance profiles per model and sequence-length histograms. for dedicated we can share more telemetry under NDA.
[05:06] Marco Ruiz: security and data retention - we need SOC2 and ability to purge logs within 30 days, and support for customer-managed keys.
[05:14] Alex Chen: Redwood supports SOC2 Type II, ISO27001; we offer customer-managed KMS and configurable retention. i'll include the security pack after the call.
[05:22] Priya Natarajan: and SSO?
[05:24] Samir Patel: SAML/SCIM for user provisioning, RBAC support.
[05:28] [00:05:28] Dana Lee: any gotchas on PII in prompts? we want guaranteed non-training of models on our data.
[05:35] Alex Chen: hosted API by default does not use customer prompts to re-train open models; we have contractual controls and for stricter needs Private deployment with on-premises control is recommended. we'll send the data usage language.
[05:47] Marco Ruiz: latency numbers - can you share p50/p95 for the model you demoed?
[05:51] Samir Patel: for redwood-mini-chat-v1 on hosted GPU pool, typical p50 for 64-token responses is ~120-180ms, p95 ~400-550ms depending on region and load. these are ballpark; we can run a benchmark with your traffic.
[06:09] Priya Natarajan: ok that could be borderline; our target p95 is 300ms. if you hit 400-550 that's above. what about Dedicated?
[06:18] Alex Chen: Dedicated reduces variance - reserved GPU pools, pinned capacity, and predictable kernel selection. we can model expected p95 given your qps and prompt length and propose a config.
[06:29] Dana Lee: cost question - are we billed per token? any hidden network egress charges?
[06:33] Alex Chen: hosted is usage-based per token for input/output. there are no hidden egress fees in the API bill, but if you replicate logs to a customer S3 or partner region there might be cloud provider charges. we'll include cost examples.
[06:48] [00:06:48] Marco Ruiz: about retries again - if we get partial stream and we reconnect, does Redwood provide a resume token? we don't want partial duplicates.
[06:57] Samir Patel: we have a streaming resume mechanism for some SDKs - you can resume from last confirmed token id, but that's SDK-specific. otherwise use idempotency keys and application-level dedupe.
[07:10] Priya Natarajan: are there examples for implementing exponential backoff?
[07:13] Samir Patel: yes we include recommended patterns in the SDK docs and the sample benchmark script Samir will share.
[07:22] Alex Chen: (minor chatter) - we also have auto-retries for transient infra errors, but we cap to avoid duplicates.
[07:30] [00:07:30] Priya Natarajan: what about rate limits during spikes? we expect sudden bursts from clients.
[07:36] Alex Chen: Hosted has soft limits per account; you can request higher throughput or reserve bursts. Dedicated gives burst capacity and more linear scaling. we also support token-level rate limiting and queue prioritization.
[07:50] Dana Lee: is there a way to guarantee ordering for streamed events? sometimes our clients mis-handle out-of-order chunks.
[07:56] Samir Patel: stream chunks include monotonically increasing sequence ids so SDKs can reorder/verify. plain HTTP chunking usually maintains order but networks can produce reorder; seq ids help.
[08:08] [00:08:08] Alex Chen: quick demo of retry headers - sample response includes x-request-id, Retry-After, and rate-limit buckets. you can rely on these to implement backoff.
[08:19] Marco Ruiz: ok. small question - what's the minimum latency overhead of TLS termination in hosted? we deploy globally and care about edge latency.
[08:28] Samir Patel: we terminate at cloud edge points-of-presence; typical overhead is low, under 10-15ms extra. region and networking will dominate.
[08:41] Priya Natarajan: if we run a pilot, can we run in a specific region? we prefer US-West.
[08:46] Alex Chen: yes - you can pick region. for Dedicated we can pin GPUs in region.
[08:51] [00:08:51] Dana Lee: integrations - any native SDK for Go? our stack is Go + Node.
[08:56] Samir Patel: yes Go and Node SDKs. plus Python and Java. SDKs handle streaming and resume logic for you.
[09:03] Marco Ruiz: any limit on prompt length? we sometimes send 8k tokens of context.
[09:08] Samir Patel: hosted supports up to 32k tokens on select models; cost and latency scale. for very large contexts we recommend chunking and summarization or using KV cache.
[09:20] Priya Natarajan: can we pin models and versions? we need stable behavior for regression testing.
[09:25] Alex Chen: yes, model version pinning and rollout controls - you can pin to exact model hash and control canary percentages in the console.
[09:33] [00:09:33] Dana Lee: are there guardrails for hallucinations?
[09:36] Samir Patel: we provide evaluation tooling in Optimize to run test suites over prompt sets and alert on quality regressions. also function calling and grounding to customer content reduce hallucination surface.
[09:47] Marco Ruiz: great. what's included in the security pack?
[09:50] Alex Chen: SOC2 report, pen test summary, data flow diagrams, retention policies, KMS integration guide, and SLA draft. we'll send those shortly.
[09:59] Priya Natarajan: thanks. what's the expected timeline to get a pilot running after we sign?
[10:04] Alex Chen: we can start a hosted pilot within a few days; Dedicated pilot takes longer for capacity planning (1-2 weeks commonly).
[10:13] [00:10:13] Samir Patel: i want to highlight SDK retry examples and the sample benchmark script i'll attach - it simulates your traffic pattern and measures p50/p95 for chosen model.
[10:23] Marco Ruiz: perfect, that will answer a lot.
[10:26] Dana Lee: any SLAs on latency?
[10:29] Alex Chen: hosted has uptime SLAs; latency SLAs are available on Dedicated/Enterprise plans. for hosted we'll provide SLO guidance and work with you to hit targets in pilot.
[10:41] Priya Natarajan: one more - can we redact PII at ingestion time?
[10:45] Samir Patel: yes, we have pre-ingest redaction hooks and can strip or tokenise fields; we also support on-prem redaction for Private deployments.
[10:53] [00:10:53] Alex Chen: ok wrapping up. recap: we'll share pricing + security pack, Samir will send benchmark script + SDK examples, and Quantify Labs will provide sample prompts and traffic profile. let's schedule a POC kickoff week of 6/8.
[11:08] Priya Natarajan: sounds good. any immediate blockers?
[11:11] Marco Ruiz: none from my side. i want to run the benchmark asap.
[11:14] Dana Lee: same.
[11:16] Alex Chen: awesome. thanks everyone, we'll follow up with next steps.
[11:20] [call ends]
